issues.item: Threat: Intrusion Monitoring: I listen for sounds that might mean someone is entering my home
issues.explanation: For toxic chemical exposure, 'listen for sounds that might mean someone is entering my home' implies an interpersonal/home-intrusion threat context that does not fit the stated trauma type and is not supported by the other selected items, which center on contamination/body danger and intrusive sensory reliving.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Escape Route Planning: always plan an escape route before entering a place
issues.explanation: 'Always plan an escape route before entering a place' is not impossible after chemical exposure, but here it reads as preparation for assault/entrapment rather than avoidance of fumes, contamination, or bodily symptoms; it is weakly aligned with the rest of the profile and the trauma context.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Lost Community: I have lost my connection to my community and culture
issues.explanation: The negative appraisal items focus strongly on social/cultural disconnection and not belonging, which is difficult to reconcile as the central appraisal pattern for a 60-year-old male whose trauma was toxic chemical exposure. These appraisals are not impossible, but alongside the rest of the profile they are poorly connected to the main symptom pattern of somatic threat, false alarms, and sensory reliving. A clinician would question why chemically exposure-related PTSD is expressed mainly as community/cultural alienation rather than danger, contamination, mistrust of body, or permanent harm beliefs.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Belong Nowhere: I no longer belong anywhere
issues.explanation: Within the selected nodes, the profile is dominated by body-based threat and intrusive sensory memory, but the maladaptive strategy item 'Avoid Reminders: Being reminded of the event by others' is not well supported because the formulation shows Triggers disconnected from all other nodes. Reminder-based avoidance centered on external prompts by others implies a trigger-driven maintenance pattern that is not reflected in the formulation or elsewhere in the self-report.

vignette:
Khan, a 60-year-old South Eastern Asian man who had worked for many years as a hotel manager, came to treatment after months of feeling unable to settle back into ordinary life with his partner. The event he described had happened at work, in the setting that had once felt most orderly and predictable to him. A chemical leak in the hotel’s maintenance area exposed him to a toxic substance before he understood what was happening. He remembered the moment in fragments that still arrived without warning: the sharp, bitter taste that seemed to flood his mouth as soon as he was near it, the sudden sense that something was dangerously wrong, and the shock of not being able to do anything useful except get himself away from the area. Even now, when the memory forced its way into his mind, he said it did not come as a story from the past but as something that seemed to happen again in the present, with the taste returning so vividly that he would briefly feel transported back into that scene. What frightened him most was the feeling that his body had failed him in a way he could not anticipate or control. He had come to believe that he could not stop bad things from happening to him, no matter how careful he tried to be.

In the weeks after the exposure, Khan began to move through his days as if danger might be waiting in ordinary places. At work, he found himself constantly scanning hallways, service corridors, and storage areas for signs that something had gone wrong. If a delivery was late, or a repair took longer than expected, he immediately assumed that something bad was happening somewhere out of sight. When guests or staff mentioned the incident, or when anyone referred to chemicals, cleaning supplies, or ventilation, he felt a rush of discomfort and pulled away from the conversation. He started avoiding reminders whenever he could, stepping out of meetings if the topic turned to maintenance or safety procedures, and changing the subject when others brought up the exposure as though speaking of it casually. These moments left him feeling exposed and ashamed, as though his body and his work no longer belonged to him in the way they once had.

At the same time, he became preoccupied with his own physical state. Khan said he constantly checked his body for signs of danger or injury, reading every throat sensation, chest tightness, or stomach feeling as though it might be the first warning of another toxic event. He watched himself closely for changes and often found that his body felt tense and ready to react before anything had actually happened. In the hotel, this meant that he could be standing at the front desk or walking through the lobby while part of his attention was still fixed on whether he felt “normal” inside. When a guest was delayed, or a maintenance report did not arrive on time, he would feel his body brace as if something threatening were about to unfold. He described these reactions as false alarms that arrived with little warning, leaving him startled by his own body’s urgency. Over time, the strain of staying on guard made everyday interactions more exhausting, and his partner noticed that he was less present at home, often distracted and difficult to reassure.

Khan’s relationship with his own body had also changed in a more painful way. He said he could no longer trust it, because it seemed capable of turning against him without notice. That belief was strongest on days when he felt a twinge of nausea, a tightening in his throat, or a wave of heat in his chest; instead of passing over these sensations, he treated them as signs that something was wrong. The result was a constant readiness, as though he needed to be prepared for an emergency at any moment. He found himself checking the environment before entering rooms, watching people’s faces for signs of alarm, and keeping track of exits and staff movements in a way that made the hotel, once familiar and competently managed, feel unpredictable. At home, he was no easier to settle. He said he no longer felt that he belonged anywhere in the way he once had, not fully at work and not comfortably at ease even in the relationship that had sustained him. The feeling of being out of place carried a quiet sadness, and it made him less willing to explain what was happening to him.

By the time he sought help, Khan was exhausted by the combination of intrusive memory, constant alertness, and the conviction that his body could not be relied upon. What brought him in finally was the fear that he could not keep functioning at work if every delay, every mention of the incident, and every unfamiliar taste or bodily sensation continued to pull him back into that exposure. He hoped treatment might help him feel safe in his own body again, but he was most afraid that the sense of danger would never fully leave him and that he would remain someone who no longer knew where he belonged.
